title: Adverb Clauses
subtitle: when, because, even though, if, unless

items.text: The first time I met your parents at the party for Nicholas and his girlfriend.
items.why: Only an adverb clause. No main clause.
items.fix: The first time I met your parents was at the party for Nicholas and his girlfriend.

items.text: After the movie ended. The audience stayed in their seats for a few minutes.
items.why: Join the clause to the main clause.
items.fix: After the movie ended, the audience stayed in their seats for a few minutes.

items.text: Whenever Josh died, his family was very sad.
items.fix: When Josh died, his family was very sad.

items.text: Because Rosa inherited a large amount of money from her parents, she was an only child.
items.fix: Because Rosa was an only child, she inherited a large amount of money from her parents.

items.text: Now that I graduated, I need to look for a job.
items.fix: Now that I have graduated, I need to look for a job.

items.text: Even though the movie is very popular, I don't think the theater will be crowded.
While some people enjoy being online a lot, others do.
items.fix: While some people enjoy being online a lot, others don't.

items.text: If anyone needs me, I'll be in my office.
Are you coming with us? If so, could you hurry?
items.why: If so = if you are coming.

items.text: Even if he invites me to the party, I will go.
items.why: even if → the result doesn't change.
items.fix: Even if he invites me to the party, I won't go.

items.text: In case you've forgotten anything, I can always send it to you.
Unless you get below 70% on the next test, you'll pass the course.
Only if Abdul's foot is better he can play in the soccer match next month.
items.why: Only if first → can he play.
items.fix: Only if Abdul's foot is better can he play in the soccer match next month.

items.title: When? Why? If what?
lines: An adverb clause answers these. It can't stand alone.
chips: when the phone rang (time)
because he was sleepy (cause)
although it was crowded (contrast)
if the weather is bad (condition)

items.title: Clause first? Use a comma
lines: Clause second? Usually no comma.
chips: When the phone rang, the baby woke up.
The baby woke up when the phone rang.

items.text: Which is correct?
options: As soon as the plane landed a blizzard began.
As soon as the plane landed, a blizzard began.

items.title: Never alone
lines: Join it to a main clause.
chips: ❌ When we were in New York. We saw several plays.
✅ When we were in New York, we saw several plays.
❌ He went to bed. Because he was sleepy.

items.text: “After the movie ended. The audience stayed in their seats.”
options: Correct
Wrong: the first part is not a sentence.
items.why: After the movie ended, the audience stayed…

lines: Adverb clause + comma + main clause. / Main clause + adverb clause (no comma).
An adverb clause can't be a sentence by itself.

examples.text: When the phone rang, the baby woke up.
The baby woke up when the phone rang.
Because he was sleepy, he went to bed.

items.text: When the door slammed.
items.why: An adverb clause can't stand alone.
items.fix: I woke up when the door slammed.

items.text: I woke up. When the door slammed.
items.why: Join the clause to the main clause.
items.fix: I woke up when the door slammed.

items.text: I woke up when the door slammed.
items.why: Main clause + adverb clause, no comma.

items.text: When the door slammed, I woke up.
The door slammed. I woke up.
After I texted you, my phone died.
The last time I texted you, and you didn't answer.
items.why: No and after an adverb clause.
items.fix: The last time I texted you, you didn't answer.

items.text: Every time the phone rings, and no one is there.
items.why: No and after an adverb clause.
items.fix: Every time the phone rings, no one is there.

items.text: Whenever the phone rings, no one is there.
As soon as we sit down to dinner, a telemarketer calls.

items.word: When Adolfo came to Chicago he planned to stay with his cousins.
Adolfo planned to stay with his cousins when he came to Chicago.
As soon as the plane landed a blizzard began.
A blizzard began as soon as the plane landed.
Once the plane landed a blizzard began.
Adolfo didn't go outside the airport until it stopped.
When it stopped Adolfo went outside.
When he went outside there weren't any taxis.
He was stranded at the airport until the roads were cleared.
As soon as the roads were cleared he left the airport.

items.text: Paulo's legs are paralyzed when he plays he moves around the basketball court in a wheelchair
options: Paulo's legs are paralyzed when he plays. He moves around the basketball court in a wheelchair.
Paulo's legs are paralyzed. When he plays, he moves around the basketball court in a wheelchair.
items.why: When he plays belongs to the second sentence.

items.text: Paulo is a member of a championship basketball team he is a wheelchair athlete
options: Paulo is a member of a championship basketball team. He is a wheelchair athlete.
Paulo is a member of a championship basketball team, he is a wheelchair athlete.

items.text: whenever his owner needs to go downtown Fritz assists him
options: Whenever his owner needs to go downtown. Fritz assists him.
Whenever his owner needs to go downtown, Fritz assists him.

items.text: Fritz can help him cross streets get on buses go down stairs and avoid obstacles
options: Fritz can help him cross streets, get on buses, go down stairs, and avoid obstacles.
Fritz can help him cross streets get on buses, go down stairs and, avoid obstacles.

items.text: sometimes when people speak to someone who is hard of hearing they shout
options: Sometimes when people speak, to someone who is hard of hearing they shout.
Sometimes when people speak to someone who is hard of hearing, they shout.
items.why: The comma comes at the end of the whole clause.

items.text: shouting is not necessary it is important to face the person and speak clearly
options: Shouting is not necessary. It is important to face the person and speak clearly.
Shouting is not necessary, it is important to face the person, and speak clearly.

items.text: The first time I met your parents at the party for Nicholas and his girlfriend.
items.why: Only an adverb clause. No main clause.
items.fix: The first time I met your parents was at the party for Nicholas and his girlfriend.

items.text: After the movie ended. The audience stayed in their seats for a few minutes.
items.why: Join the clause to the main clause.
items.fix: After the movie ended, the audience stayed in their seats for a few minutes.

levels.title: After, until, by the time
levels.full: Using Adverb Clauses to Show Time Relationships

items.title: Many time words
lines: Each one shows a different time relationship.
chips: after / before
when = at that time
while / as = during that time
since = from then until now
until / till = to that time, then stop
as soon as / once = right after
whenever / every time
the first / last / next time

items.title: Future? Use the present
lines: No will in the time clause.
chips: After she graduates, she will get a job.
As soon as it stops raining, we will leave.
The next time I go to New York, I'm going to see a ballet.

items.text: The next time Paul ___ to New York, he will visit the museum.
options: will fly
flies
items.why: Time clause about the future → simple present.

items.title: by the time, since
lines: by the time → perfect in the main clause. since → present perfect in the main clause.
chips: By the time he arrived, we had already left.
By the time he comes, we will have already left.
I haven't seen him since he left this morning.
I've known her ever since I was a child.

items.text: By the time you get home, I ___ dinner for you.
options: made
will have made
items.why: by the time + present → future perfect.

items.text: ___ Josh died, his family was very sad.
options: Whenever
When
items.why: It happened once → when, not whenever.

lines: Time clause about the future: simple present (no will).
by the time → had done / will have done. since → have done.

examples.text: After she graduates, she will get a job.
By the time he arrived, we had already left.
I've known her ever since I was a child.

items.text: Oscar can't catch the meaning. People speak English too fast. (when)
options: Oscar can't catch the meaning, when people speak English too fast.
Oscar can't catch the meaning when people speak English too fast.

items.text: The teacher speaks too fast. Oscar is going to ask her to slow down. (the next time)
options: The next time the teacher speaks too fast, Oscar is going to ask her to slow down.
The next time the teacher will speak too fast, Oscar is going to ask her to slow down.
items.why: No will in a time clause.

items.text: Oscar is listening to English. He tries not to translate. (while)
options: While Oscar is listening to English he tries, not to translate from his language.
While Oscar is listening to English, he tries not to translate from his language.

items.text: His teacher encourages students to figure out the meaning. They check their dictionaries. (before)
options: His teacher encourages students to figure out the meaning before they check their dictionaries.
Before his teacher encourages students to figure out the meaning, they check their dictionaries.
items.why: First figure it out, then check.

items.text: Oscar began studying English. He has wanted to speak fluently. (ever since)
options: Ever since Oscar has wanted to speak fluently, he began studying English.
Ever since Oscar began studying English, he has wanted to speak fluently.
items.why: ever since + past, main clause present perfect.

items.text: I will call you before I ___ over.
I will go to bed after I ___ my homework.
I did my chores before I ___ to my friend's house.
By the time you get home, I ___ dinner for you.
items.why: by the time + present → future perfect.

missions.title: Dogs, spiders, passwords; Marco and Anya

items.text: Ever since I was a child, I ___ afraid of dogs.
One time a small dog bit me when I ___ it.
Whenever I ___ spiders, I scream.
A spider fell out of my shoe as I ___ it on this morning.
items.why: as = during that time → past progressive.

items.text: By the time I stopped screaming, the spider ___.
items.why: by the time + past → past perfect.

items.text: The last time I ___ overseas, I lost my passport.
The next time I ___, I'm going to bring a photocopy of it.
The first time Marco was asked, “How's it going?” ___
options: he thought the person was asking about leaving.
he will think the person asks about leaving.
items.ctx: Marco and Anya have had some funny misunderstandings in their new country.

items.text: At first, every time someone asked Anya how she was, ___
options: she has given a long answer.
she gave a long answer.

items.text: The next time Marco wants to get the server's attention, ___
options: he won't snap his fingers.
he didn't snap his fingers.

items.text: The baggage will be loaded soon. The plane will take off. (as soon as)
options: As soon as the baggage will be loaded, the plane will take off.
As soon as the baggage is loaded, the plane will take off.
items.why: No will in a time clause.

items.text: The passengers got on the plane. The flight attendant closed the door. (after)
options: After the passengers got on the plane, the flight attendant closed the door.
After the flight attendant closed the door, the passengers got on the plane.
items.why: First they got on, then the door closed.

items.text: The passengers got on the plane. The flight attendant closed the door. (before)
options: Before the passengers got on the plane, the flight attendant closed the door.
The passengers got on the plane before the flight attendant closed the door.

items.text: Malea feels nervous. She flies. (whenever)
options: Malea feels nervous whenever she flies.
Malea flies whenever she feels nervous.
items.why: whenever she flies = every time she flies.

items.text: The plane was climbing. We hit turbulence. (while)
options: While we hit turbulence, the plane was climbing.
While the plane was climbing, we hit turbulence.

items.text: I was falling asleep. The pilot made an announcement. (just as)
options: Just as I was falling asleep, the pilot made an announcement.
Just as the pilot was falling asleep, I made an announcement.
items.why: just as = at that same moment.

items.text: I fell asleep. He finished. (as soon as)
options: I fell asleep, as soon as he will finish.
I fell asleep as soon as he finished.

items.text: I stood up to walk to the restroom. The flight attendant told us to fasten our seat belts. (just after)
options: Just after I stood up to walk to the restroom, the flight attendant told us to fasten our seat belts.
Just after the flight attendant told us to fasten our seat belts, I will stand up.

items.text: We had to stay in our seats. The pilot turned off the seat belt sign. (until)
options: Until we had to stay in our seats, the pilot turned off the seat belt sign.
We had to stay in our seats until the pilot turned off the seat belt sign.
items.why: until = to that time, then no longer.

items.text: We had lunch. The person next to me has been talking non-stop. (since)
options: Since we had lunch, the person next to me has been talking non-stop.
Since we have had lunch, the person next to me talked non-stop.
items.why: since + past, main clause present perfect.

items.text: I fly. I will bring earplugs. (the next time)
options: The next time I will fly, I will bring earplugs.
The next time I fly, I will bring earplugs.
items.why: No will in a time clause.

items.text: I will text you. We land. (as soon as)
options: I will text you as soon as we land.
I will text you as soon as we will land.
items.why: No will in a time clause.

items.text: I get my bags. I will meet you in the passenger-loading zone. (just as soon as)
options: Just as soon as I got my bags, I will meet you in the passenger-loading zone.
Just as soon as I get my bags, I will meet you in the passenger-loading zone.
items.why: Future → present in the time clause.

items.text: I flew this airline. My bags were lost. (the first time)
options: The first time I flew this airline, my bags were lost.
The first time I fly this airline, my bags were lost.

items.text: I will be happy to stretch my legs. We get off the plane. (once)
options: I will be happy to stretch my legs once we will get off the plane.
I will be happy to stretch my legs once we get off the plane.
items.why: No will in a time clause.

items.text: We land. We will have been on the plane for ten hours. (by the time)
options: By the time we land, we will have been on the plane for ten hours.
By the time we will land, we were on the plane for ten hours.
items.why: by the time + present → future perfect.

items.text: Before Jennifer won the lottery, she ___ any kind of contest.
options: hasn't entered
doesn't enter
wasn't entering
hadn't entered
items.why: Before a past event → past perfect.

items.text: Every time Prakash sees a movie made in India, he ___ homesick.
options: will have felt
felt
feels
is feeling

items.text: Since I left Venezuela six years ago, I ___ to visit friends and family several times.
options: return
will have returned
am returning
have returned

items.text: While he was washing his new car, Lawrence ___ some scratches on his front bumper.
options: has discovered
was discovering
is discovering
discovered
items.why: A short action during a long one → simple past.

items.text: Yesterday while I was attending a sales meeting, Matthew ___ on the company's annual report.
options: was working
had been working
has worked
works
items.why: Two actions in progress → past progressive.

items.text: Tony ___ to have children until his little daughter was born.
options: doesn't want
hadn't wanted
wasn't wanting
hasn't wanted
items.why: Before a past event → past perfect.

items.text: “I ___ on another horse as long as I live.”
options: never ride
have never ridden
will never ride
do not ride
items.why: A promise about the future → will.

items.text: The next time Paul ___ to New York, he will visit the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
options: will fly
flies
has flown
will have flown

items.text: Ever since Maurice arrived, he ___ quietly in the corner. Is something wrong?
options: sat
has been sitting
had been sitting
will have sat
items.why: ever since … until now → present perfect progressive.

items.text: After Nela ___ for 20 minutes, she began to feel tired.
options: jogging
had been jogging
has been jogging
has jogged
items.why: Before a past event → past perfect progressive.

items.text: Peter, ___ since you got home from football practice?
options: have you eaten
will you eat
are you eating
do you eat

items.text: The last time I ___ in Athens, the weather was hot and humid.
options: had been
was
am
will have been

items.text: By the time the young birds ___ the nest for good, they will have learned how to fly.
options: will leave
will have left
are leaving
leave

items.text: Just after ___
options: a thief broke into her car, Judy parked it.
Judy parked her car, a thief broke into it.
items.ctx: 4:00 Judy parked at the mall. 4:03 A thief broke into her car. 4:30 Judy returned. 4:31 She called the police. 4:35 The police arrived. 4:35 Judy began crying.

items.text: Just as ___
options: the police arrived, Judy began crying.
Judy parked her car, the police arrived.
items.ctx: 4:31 She called the police. 4:35 The police arrived. 4:35 Judy began crying.

items.text: While ___
options: Judy called the police, a thief was breaking into her car.
Judy was buying jeans, a thief broke into her car.
items.why: The thief came during her shopping.
items.ctx: 4:00 Judy went to buy jeans. 4:03 A thief broke into her car. 4:30 Judy returned.

items.text: By the time ___
options: Judy returned to her car, a thief had stolen her radio.
Judy returned to her car, a thief stole her radio at 4:30.
items.why: It was finished before she returned → past perfect.
items.ctx: 4:03 A thief stole her radio. 4:30 Judy returned.

items.text: As soon as ___
options: Judy called the police, she returned to her car.
Judy returned to her car, she called the police.
items.ctx: 4:30 Judy returned. 4:31 She called the police.

items.text: Whenever Josh died, his family was very sad.
items.fix: When Josh died, his family was very sad.

talk.title: About me
talk.task: Finish Claude's sentences: “As soon as I get up tomorrow, …”, “Ever since I was a child, …”
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Give me one sentence beginning at a time and I finish it: After I leave class today, ... / Before I go to bed tonight, ... / As soon as I get up tomorrow, ... / Whenever I feel nervous, ... / The first time I spoke English with a stranger, ... / Ever since I was a child, ... / As long as I live, ... / Just as I was falling asleep last night, .... Check my verb tenses: present (not will) in future time clauses, present perfect after ever since, past after the first time.

talk.title: A cultural misunderstanding
talk.task: Tell Claude about a time when language or culture caused a funny misunderstanding.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English writing partner. Ask me to write a short paragraph (5-6 sentences) about a cultural or language misunderstanding I have had or seen. I should use time clauses (the first time, when, until, since, whenever). Then check: commas after adverb clauses that come first, correct tenses in time clauses, and no adverb clause standing alone as a sentence.

levels.title: Because, now that, since
levels.full: Using Adverb Clauses to Show Cause and Effect

items.title: because + the cause
lines: The other clause is the effect.
chips: Because he was sleepy, he went to bed.
He went to bed because he was sleepy.
❌ Because he went to bed, he was sleepy.

items.text: Which is logical?
options: Because Rosa inherited a large amount of money, she was an only child.
Because Rosa was an only child, she inherited a large amount of money.
items.why: Only child = the cause. Money = the effect.

items.title: now that = because now
lines: Use present, present perfect, or future. Not simple past.
chips: Now that I've finished the semester, I'm going to rest a few days.
Now that he's unemployed, he can't pay his bills.

items.text: Now that I ___, I need to look for a job.
options: graduated
have graduated

items.title: since = because (a known fact)
lines: since can also mean time. Check the meaning.
chips: Since Monday is a holiday, we don't have to go to work. (because)
Since I came here, I have met many people. (time)

items.text: “Since I was young, I have been artistic.” Here, since means…
options: because
from that time until now

lines: because / since / now that + cause, + effect.
now that = because now (present time). since can also mean time.

examples.text: Because he was sleepy, he went to bed.
Now that I've finished the semester, I'm going to rest.
Since Monday is a holiday, we don't have to go to work.

items.word: Now that I've finished art school, I can focus on finding work as an illustrator.
Since I was young, I have been artistic.
Since I've had formal training, maybe I can illustrate books.
Since Monday is a holiday, we don't have to go to work.
Since I came here, I have met many people.
Since you're a good cook and I'm not, you should cook the dinner.

items.text: Because Rosa inherited a large amount of money from her parents, she was an only child.
items.why: The cause and effect are reversed.
items.fix: Because Rosa was an only child, she inherited a large amount of money from her parents.

items.text: Now that I graduated, I need to look for a job.
items.fix: Now that I have graduated, I need to look for a job.

items.text: We have a lot of frequent-flier miles. We can visit several countries. (now that)
options: Now that we have a lot of frequent-flier miles, we can visit several countries.
Now that we can visit several countries, we have a lot of frequent-flier miles.

items.text: We can compare hotel prices. They are posted online. (since)
options: Since we can compare hotel prices, they are posted online.
Since hotel prices are posted online, we can compare them.

items.text: We have read the online hotel reviews. We can choose our hotel. (now that)
options: Now that we have read the online hotel reviews, we can choose our hotel.
Now that we can choose our hotel, we have read the online hotel reviews.

items.text: There is little chance we will get lost. We have GPS on our phones. (because)
options: We have GPS on our phones because there is little chance we will get lost.
There is little chance we will get lost because we have GPS on our phones.

items.text: People post online reviews instantly. Customer service has improved. (since)
options: Since people post online reviews instantly, customer service has improved.
Since customer service has improved, people post online reviews instantly.

items.text: We won't get so homesick. We can video chat with our families. (because)
options: We can video chat with our families because we won't get so homesick.
We won't get so homesick because we can video chat with our families.

items.word: Because my grandfather has died, my mom would like my grandmother to move in with us.
Because my grandmother lives alone, I visit her more often.
Because my grandmother was a nurse, she took good care of her health.
Because my grandparents saved for their retirement, she doesn't need to worry about finances.
Because she is 90, I have asked her a few times if she should continue driving.

items.text: Because my grandmother lives alone, I visit her more often. →
options: Now that my grandmother lives alone, I visit her more often.
Now that my grandmother lived alone, I visit her more often.

items.text: Because she is 90, I have asked her if she should continue driving. →
options: Now that she was 90, I have asked her if she should continue driving.
Now that she is 90, I have asked her if she should continue driving.

levels.title: Even though…
levels.full: Expressing Contrast (Unexpected Result): Using Even Though

items.title: because vs. even though
lines: because → the result you expect.
even though → a surprise.
chips: Because the weather was cold, I didn't go swimming.
Even though the weather was cold, I went swimming.

items.text: Even though I was very tired, I ___.
options: went to bed early
stayed up late
items.why: Tired, but stayed up = a surprise.

items.title: Same commas as because
lines: Clause first → comma.
chips: Even though I wasn't tired, I went to bed.
I went to bed even though I wasn't tired.
items.tip: although and though mean the same.

items.text: Tim's in good shape physically ___ he doesn't get much exercise.
options: because
even though
items.why: No exercise but good shape = a surprise.

items.text: Even though the movie is very popular, I ___ the theater will be crowded.
options: think
don't think
items.why: Popular but not crowded = a surprise.

lines: because + cause → expected result.
even though + fact → unexpected result.

examples.text: Because the weather was cold, I didn't go swimming.
Even though the weather was cold, I went swimming.

items.text: Because it was a dark, cloudy day, ___.
options: I didn't put on my sunglasses
I put on my sunglasses

items.text: Even though it was a dark, cloudy day, ___.
options: I put on my sunglasses
I didn't put on my sunglasses

items.text: Even though Mira was cold, ___.
options: she wore a heavy coat outside
she wore a light sweater outside
items.why: Cold but a light sweater = a surprise.

items.text: Because Mira enjoys the outdoors, ___.
options: she goes for walks rain or shine
she doesn't go for walks in bad weather
items.why: Loves outdoors → walks in any weather.

items.text: Which sentence expresses an unexpected result?
options: Because I was very tired, I went to bed early.
Even though I was very tired, I stayed up late.

items.text: Even though the movie is very popular, I don't think the theater will be crowded.
Even though I studied hard, I passed the test.
items.why: Studying → passing is expected: use because.
items.fix: Because I studied hard, I passed the test.

items.text: Barry's in good shape physically ___ he gets a lot of exercise.
options: because
even though

items.text: ___ Yoko has a job, she is able to pay her rent and feed her family.
options: Because
Even though

items.text: ___ Melissa has a job, she doesn't make enough money to support her four children.
options: Because
Even though
items.why: A job but not enough money = a surprise.

items.text: Joe speaks Spanish well ___ he lived in Mexico for a year.
options: because
even though

items.text: Sherry didn't learn Spanish ___ she lived in Mexico for a year.
options: because
even though
items.why: Lived there but didn't learn = a surprise.

items.text: Jin jumped into the river to rescue a little girl ___ he wasn't a good swimmer.
options: because
even though
items.why: Not a good swimmer but jumped = a surprise.

items.text: ___ she was rescued right away, the girl survived.
options: Because
Even though

items.text: ___ the flood washed away the bridge, the campers were able to cross the river…
options: Because
Even though
items.why: No bridge but they crossed = a surprise.

items.text: …the campers were able to cross the river ___ they had a boat.
options: because
even though

items.text: ___ the bridge was out of service for several months, people had to find alternate ways to get across.
options: Because
Even though

items.text: It was raining. Did you go to the zoo anyway?
options: Yes. Even though it was raining, I went to the zoo.
No. Even though it was raining, I didn't go to the zoo.

items.text: You studied hard. Did you pass the test?
options: Yes. Even though I studied hard, I passed the test.
No. Even though I studied hard, I didn't pass the test.

items.text: You stayed up all night. Did you go to work?
options: Yes. Even though I stayed up all night, I went to work.
No. Even though I stayed up all night, I didn't go to work.
items.why: No sleep but worked = the surprise.

items.text: The food was terrible. Did you eat it anyway?
options: No. Even though the food was terrible, I didn't eat it.
Yes. Even though the food was terrible, I ate it.
items.why: Terrible but ate it = the surprise.

items.text: You didn't study. Did you pass the test anyway?
options: Yes. Even though I didn't study, I passed the test.
No. Even though I didn't study, I didn't pass the test.
items.why: No study but passed = the surprise.

items.text: You fell down the stairs. Did you get hurt?
options: Yes. Even though I fell down the stairs, I got hurt.
No. Even though I fell down the stairs, I didn't get hurt.
items.why: Fell but not hurt = the surprise.

items.text: You bought a brand-new air conditioner. Does it work?
options: No. Even though I bought a brand-new air conditioner, it doesn't work.
Yes. Even though I bought a brand-new air conditioner, it works.

items.text: Your grandfather is 100 years old. Is he still young at heart?
options: No. Even though my grandfather is 100 years old, he isn't young at heart.
Yes. Even though my grandfather is 100 years old, he is still young at heart.

talk.title: Yes, even though…

items.text: If you don't stay in bed and rest, you won't recover quickly from the virus.
options: You won't recover quickly from the virus unless you stay in bed and rest.
You will recover quickly from the virus unless you stay in bed and rest.

items.text: If you don't see the doctor in person, she won't give you a prescription.
options: The doctor won't give you a prescription only if you see her in person.
The doctor will give you a prescription only if you see her in person.

items.text: If you don't have a fever, you can go back to work.
options: You can go back to work unless you have a fever.
You can't go back to work unless you don't have a fever.
items.why: if you don't = unless you do.

items.text: If you don't have a doctor's note, you can't take sick time.
options: You can take sick time only if you don't have a doctor's note.
You can take sick time only if you have a doctor's note.
items.why: The note is the one condition.

items.text: If you don't call the pharmacy now, your prescription won't be ready on time.
options: Your prescription won't be ready on time unless you call the pharmacy now.
Your prescription will be ready on time unless you call the pharmacy now.

items.text: If you don't take your medicine, you won't get well quickly.
options: You will get well quickly only if you won't take your medicine.
You will get well quickly only if you take your medicine.

items.text: Only if Abdul's foot is better he can play in the soccer match next month.
items.why: Only if first → can he play.
items.fix: Only if Abdul's foot is better can he play in the soccer match next month.

levels.title: Clause mix
levels.full: Chapter 17 Review: The Party, How People Learn

items.title: Four jobs
lines: Time, cause, contrast, condition.

items.text: It may or may not rain. ___ it rains, the party will be held outdoors.
options: Unless
Only if
items.why: Unless it rains = if it doesn't rain → outdoors.

items.title: Move the clause around
lines: Good writers don't always start with the adverb clause.
chips: When I am involved, I learn best.
I learn best when I am involved.

items.text: I often forget the meanings of new words ___ I use them right away.
options: unless
only if

items.text: I remember new words best ___ I write them in a sentence.
options: when
unless
items.why: A time / condition that helps → when.

lines: Pick the connector by meaning: time, cause, contrast, or condition.
Clause first → comma. Present tense (not will) for future time and conditions.

examples.text: Unless it rains, the party will be held outdoors.
The party will be held indoors only if it rains.

missions.title: The party: rain or no rain

items.text: If ___
options: it rains, the party will be held indoors.
it will rain, the party will be held indoors.
items.ctx: It may or may not rain. The party will be held indoors or outdoors.

items.text: Even if ___
options: it rains, the party will be held indoors.
it rains, the party will be held outdoors.
items.why: even if = rain won't change the plan.

items.text: Whether or not ___
options: it rains, the party will be held outdoors.
it rains, the party will be canceled if it's sunny.
items.why: Rain or not: the same result.

items.text: In case ___
options: it will rain, the party is held indoors yesterday.
it rains, the party will be held indoors.

items.text: Unless ___
options: it rains, the party will be held outdoors.
it rains, the party will be held indoors.
items.why: unless it rains = if it doesn't rain.

items.text: Only if ___
options: it rains the party will be held indoors.
it rains will the party be held indoors.

items.text: There is not one answer since much depends on individual learning styles.
options: because
from that time
items.ctx: “Tell me and I forget. Teach me and I remember. Involve me and I learn.” — Benjamin Franklin

items.text: Before you ever pick up a piece of paper, the person says the following…
options: simple present
future with will
items.ask: What tense is in the adverb clause?

items.text: How well are you going to learn so long as the instructor continues in this manner?
options: during all that time
because
items.why: so long as = as long as.

items.text: Your instructor gives the directions while she folds the paper herself.
options: during that time
the exact opposite

items.text: Every time she gives you instructions, both you and she fold your own papers.
options: whenever
only once

items.text: Which method involves the learner most?
options: Only listening to the steps.
Watching the instructor fold.
Folding your own paper at each step.

items.text: ___ we pay our bills, we'll have little money left over for the holidays.
options: Once
Unless

items.text: ___ I get a promotion to manager, I won't relocate to another city.
options: Even
Even if
items.why: even needs if before a clause.

items.text: I care about you ___ you believe me.
options: if or not
whether or not

items.text: If tenants ___ any questions about the apartment, they need to contact the manager.
options: will have
have

items.text: ___ I've finished the semester, I'm going to rest a few days.
options: Now that
Unless

items.text: Mary is rich, ___ John is poor.
options: while
because

items.text: ___ the weather was cold, I went swimming.
options: Because
Even though

items.text: I'll go swimming tomorrow ___ it's cold.
options: unless
in case

items.text: We'll have been on the plane for ten hours ___ we land.
options: by the time
since
items.why: Finished before that moment → by the time.

talk.title: How I learn best
talk.task: Finish Claude's sentences about learning vocabulary: “I remember new words best when…”
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English writing partner. Give me one sentence beginning at a time about learning English vocabulary and I complete it: I remember new words best when ... / I often forget the meanings of new words unless ... / Even if I ... / I ... only if ... / If students want to increase their vocabulary, ... / Although ... / When I am involved in my learning, I feel .... Then ask me to join three of my sentences into a short paragraph. Check: comma after an adverb clause that comes first, even if (not even), and inversion after Only if at the start.

items.text: Once we [will pay] our bills, we'll have little money left over for the holidays.
options: Once we pay our bills, we'll have little money left over for the holidays.
Once we paid our bills, we'll have little money left over for the holidays.
Once we are pay our bills, we'll have little money left over for the holidays.
items.why: No will in a time clause.

items.text: [In the case] there is an emergency, call the number on this paper.
options: In case of there is an emergency, call the number on this paper.
In case there is an emergency, call the number on this paper.
In the case that is an emergency, call the number on this paper.

items.text: Unless you have a doctor's note, you [can] take sick time from work.
options: Unless you have a doctor's note, you could take sick time from work.
Unless you have a doctor's note, you can to take sick time from work.
Unless you have a doctor's note, you can't take sick time from work.

items.text: If tenants [will have] any questions about the apartment, they need to contact the manager.
options: If tenants have any questions about the apartment, they need to contact the manager.
If tenants had any questions about the apartment, they need to contact the manager.
If tenants are having any questions about the apartment, they need to contact the manager.

items.text: Only if you help me [I will] clean the apartment.
options: Only if you help me, I will clean the apartment.
Only if you help me will I clean the apartment.
Only if you help me I clean will the apartment.

items.text: [When Yusef finished] medical school at the age of 21.
options: When Yusef finishing medical school at the age of 21.
When Yusef had finished medical school at the age of 21.
Yusef finished medical school at the age of 21.
items.why: A when-clause alone is not a sentence.

items.text: [Even I get] a promotion to manager, I won't relocate to another city.
options: Even if I get a promotion to manager, I won't relocate to another city.
Even I will get a promotion to manager, I won't relocate to another city.
Even though if I get a promotion to manager, I won't relocate to another city.

items.text: I care about you [if or not] you believe me.
options: I care about you if not you believe me.
I care about you whether or not you believe me.
I care about you even or not you believe me.

items.text: [Whenever] Josh died, his family was very sad.
options: Every time Josh died, his family was very sad.
Until Josh died, his family was very sad.
When Josh died, his family was very sad.

items.text: Now that I [graduated], I need to look for a job.
options: Now that I have graduated, I need to look for a job.
Now that I had graduated, I need to look for a job.
Now that I was graduating, I need to look for a job.

items.text: While some people enjoy being online a lot, others [do].
options: While some people enjoy being online a lot, others are.
While some people enjoy being online a lot, others don't.
While some people enjoy being online a lot, others do too.

items.text: Even if he invites me to the party, I [will] go.
options: Even if he invites me to the party, I would go.
Even if he invites me to the party, I am going.
Even if he invites me to the party, I won't go.
items.why: even if → the result doesn't change.
